item.title: Lightyears lands funding boost to accelerate NZ solar and battery builds
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian renewables financing firm Infradebt will pump more than $80 million in renewables developer Lightyears to accelerate the roll out of more than 300 MW of solar and battery projects across New Zealand.
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand renewables developer Lightyears has secured almost 140 million (NZD 174 million) from Australian and Japanese backers to fund the delivery of more than 300 MW of utility-scale solar and battery energy storage projects across the country over the next five years.

Canberra-based renewables financing firm Infradebt confirmed it will provide Lightyears with an $80 million (NZD 100 million) lending facility. The new funding also includes a $59.4 million (NZD 74 million) planned investment from Japanese construction group Obayashi Corporation.

Lightyears Managing Director and co-founder Matt Shanks said the capital injection would give the company the capacity to take on more projects, with a target of delivering more than 300 MW of utility-scale solar and battery energy storage infrastructure over the next five years.

“This capital gives us a clear runway to deliver power projects up and down the nation,” he said. “And that level of capital injection allows us to take on more projects concurrently. That is more locally generated renewable electricity and stronger energy resilience for Kiwi communities and the businesses that need it.” 

Lightyears has focused on smaller-scale solar projects with the 13.5 MW Reefton Solar Farm being built on the on the West Coast of New Zealand’s South Island, the company’s largest project to date. The company said it has another 21 MW of projects under construction, as well as a development pipeline of 28 projects totalling about 338 MW.

It’s seven operational facilities include the 2.4 MW Waiuku and the 4.7 MW Carterton solar farms on New Zealand’s North Island, and the 7.2 MW Ashburton and 5 MW Waimakariri solar farms on the South Island.

Shanks said Lightyears’ solar farms are designed to fit the scale and character of local landscapes and are intended to integrate with surrounding land uses.

“We complement the larger-scale solar farms, slotting into communities around the country and connecting to the local distribution networks,” he said. “The size of our solar farms also mean they can be constructed quickly to provide renewable energy to the grid at a time when it’s desperately needed.”

Shanks said Infradebt and Obayashi are ideal partners to support the next phase of growth for the Lightyears energy platform.

“This funding lets us add new generation in the regions that need it,” he said.

Under the agreement, Obayashi will take a 90% stake in a new company called LYOC1, that will hold the solar projects. It will invest in stages as each project reaches development milestones.

The InfraDebt loan builds on the company’s existing relationship with Lightyears.

“New Zealand is a market we like, and we intend to be here for the long term, continuing to grow our relationship with Lightyears while deepening our presence on both the lending and investor side,” InfraDebt Investment Director and co-founder Chin-Lee Yu said.

item.title: Real cost of charging an EV from surplus solar
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Rooftop generation can make EV charging inexpensive, but a fair comparison must count the solar-export income forgone, the grid alternative and the electricity actually available to the car.
item.content:encoded:
An electric vehicle (EV) charging beneath a solar-equipped roof can appear to be running for free. There is no petrol purchase, and the solar electricity does not create a grid-energy charge. But that electricity may otherwise have earned the household a feed-in credit. Where export is the alternative, using it in the car means giving up that income.

That does not make solar charging a bad deal. It changes the question: how much does using the surplus save compared with the charging option the household would otherwise choose?

Three ways to supply the same 100 km

Consider a hypothetical EV requiring 18 kWh from the household AC electricity supply to travel 100 kilometres. This assumption already includes EV charging losses and is held constant across the comparison. It is not a measured vehicle result or an Australian fleet average.

Assume ordinary grid electricity costs 30c/kWh, an available off-peak rate is 10c/kWh, and surplus solar would earn a 5c/kWh feed-in tariff. All rates are illustrative, not current retailer offers. Import prices include GST; export credits are used as stated. No home battery is involved.

The solar figure is not a retailer charge. It is the $0.90 export credit the household gives up. Under these assumptions, solar charging saves $4.50 per 100 km compared with ordinary grid charging after accounting for forgone exports, but only $0.90 compared with off-peak charging.

These are marginal energy comparisons, not total ownership costs. They exclude solar and charger purchase, installation, maintenance, financing, daily supply charges and any change in demand charges. A decision to buy equipment needs a separate assessment.

A mixture is more useful than an all-solar promise

Suppose half the required energy comes directly from surplus solar and half is bought off-peak. The calculation becomes 9 kWh × $0.05 plus 9 kWh × $0.10: $1.35 per 100 km. Of that, $0.90 is a grid-energy charge and $0.45 is forgone export income.

Compared with supplying all 18 kWh off-peak for $1.80, the benefit is $0.45 – not the $4.05 difference against ordinary grid charging. Both comparisons are mathematically valid, but only the household’s realistic alternative tells it what changing behaviour would save.

Sunshine is not the same as surplus

The available solar is what remains after other household demand. In a simplified example with no home battery, 5 kW of solar generation and 2 kW of other household load leave 3 kW for the car. A charger drawing 7 kW would still need 4 kW from the grid. The relevant grid rate is the one applying at that time.

The vehicle must also be connected while that surplus is available. Morning exports do not become a one-for-one credit for charging after sunset. A solar-aware charging system can help match charging with excess generation, but an ordinary timer alone does not guarantee solar-only charging.

The feed-in tariff can change the answer

Use the export credit that would actually apply to those kWh. Time-of-use and tiered feed-in tariffs can make a headline rate misleading. This comparison assumes self-consumption reduces paid exports; older gross-metered arrangements require a different calculation.

Holding energy needs and all other charges equal, a hypothetical 10c/kWh export credit and 10c/kWh off-peak import price produce the same $1.80 energy cost per 100 km. At a 15c export credit, using that solar for the car gives up $2.70. Exporting it and charging later for $1.80 would be $0.90 better on this narrow comparison – provided those rates and the later charging opportunity are genuinely available.

Export limits and home batteries need separate treatment

Some solar output would otherwise be curtailed because it cannot be exported. Capturing that would-be-curtailed energy can have zero forgone export income, provided there is no other valuable use for it. That applies only to the affected energy, not every kilowatt-hour generated by the system.

A home battery adds another alternative. Diverting solar into the car may leave less stored energy to avoid expensive household imports later. Charging through a battery also introduces storage losses and battery wear. The direct-solar figure above should not be presented as a stored-solar cost.

Judge the whole household bill

Before changing plans, compare the complete bill: import rates and charging windows, daily supply charges, any demand charges, export credits and eligibility conditions. IPART cautions that a higher feed-in tariff can come with higher prices elsewhere in the plan.

Use electricity bills, charger records and solar monitoring to establish when the car is home, how much energy it needs and how much surplus is available. A longer period of interval data is more useful than one sunny day; generation and household use vary across seasons.

Cheap charging is not the same as a solar-system payback result. Existing equipment and a new installation are different decisions, and any additional hardware cost must be weighed against the extra savings it enables.

The useful test is not “Did the electricity come from the roof?” It is “What would that electricity otherwise have earned or saved, and what would charging the car cost instead?”

For the assumptions here, surplus solar wins – but the size of the benefit depends on the alternative.

Author: Oliver S, Evital, a vehicle directory and research hub focused on EVs in the Australian market

item.title: EP Cube lands CEC approval for all-in-one three-phase energy storage systems
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Canadian Solar has showcased its expanding EP Cube portfolio for the Australian market, including next-generation single- and three-phase all-in-one energy storage systems that deliver increased output, expanded MPPT flexibility, and storage capacities up 200 kWh.
item.content:encoded:
EP Cube, the residential energy storage brand under Chinese-Canadian PV heavyweight Canadian Solar, has unveiled its all-in-one energy storage solutions that combine hybrid inverters with modular lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for Australia’s residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) markets.

Included in the portfolio is a recently Clean Energy Council (CEC) approved three-phase12 kW system designed for larger homes and light C&I applications.

EP Cube Sales Manager Sudeesh V said the three-phase system delivers 12 kW of continuous AC output, handles up to 24 kW of PV input across four MPPTs and capacities begin at 10 kWh of storage, using two battery units, and can scale up to 40 kWh per unit within a single stacked footprint utilising eight modules.

“For higher-capacity demands, up to five units can be paralleled for 200 kWh of total storage,” he said, adding each MPPT can accommodate PV modules with an operating current profile of up to 17 A and a short-circuit threshold of 24 A, operating across a DC voltage window up to 1,000 V.

With CEC approval and listing now in place, Sudeesh said the systems are now ready for nationwide installation, providing a reliable new option for Australian families seeking greater energy independence.

Alongside the three-phase system, EP Cube showcased its single-phase 7.6 kW system that utilises the same individual battery modules, featuring a nominal capacity of 5 kWh and weighing 43 kg.

The single-phase system provides 7.6 kW of AC output, handles up to 10 kWp of PV input, and offers 10 to 30 kWh of modular storage with built-in backup.

It is expected a next-generation version of the single-phase system will be available in Australia from Q2 next year.

Sudeesh V said the 2.0 single-phase system delivers 10 kW AC output, handles up to 15 kW PV input, and features four independent MPPTs for complex roof installations. Up to two units can be paralleled for 80 kWh of total storage capacity.

For both the single- and three-phase systems products, Canadian Solar provides 10-year warranty on the inverter unit and up to 10 years or 6,000 cycles on the LFP battery modules.

Both products are compatible with the EP Cube App, that allows customers to monitor their energy production, storage, and usage, and manage how their system operates.

Sudeesh V said for installers, the app acts as a one-stop tool for commissioning, remote diagnostics, and fleet management.

EP Cube also announced it plans to release a human machine interface (HMI) display that will complement the app. The HMI will provide at-a-glance visibility on a seven-inch wall-mounted touchscreen. It is expected to be made available in the Australian market in Q1 2027.

item.title: Samsung C&T acquires WA engineering firm Powertech in $100 million BESS play
item.dc:creator: Tristan Rayner
item.description: The South Korean giant has reportedly acquired a majority stake in Perth-headquartered electrical engineering and technical services business Powertech, securing 300 engineers and high-voltage technicians to de-risk its gigawatt-scale Australian battery storage pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
Samsung C&T has acquired a majority stake in Australian electrical engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractor Powertech in a deal valued at about $100 million (USD 70 million). The transaction surfaced via the Australian Financial Review’s Street Talk column, the quasi-clearinghouse for Australian corporate dealmaking that often runs ahead of formal market disclosures.

Citing sales documentation from advisor PwC, the report notes Powertech is forecast to generate $115 million in FY26 revenue and $8.9 million in EBITDA, valuing the buyout at roughly 11.2x EBITDA. Management will retain a minority stake.

Operating across Western Australia, Queensland, the Northern Territory, and Singapore, Powertech employs 300 engineers and technicians. The firm provides full power and electrical EPC turnkey solutions across utility-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS), switchyards, microgrids, and standalone power systems. Powertech offers everything from feasibility studies, design, construction, commissioning and start-up, and operations and maintenance. It also supplies some end-to-end EPC services for smaller scale projects.

The acquisition comes as Samsung C&T expands its ‘full-wrap’ EPC offering in the Australian market. In mid-2025 it won a full-wrap EPC contract to deliver Fotowatio Renewable Ventures (FRV) Australia’s 250 MW / 500 MWh Gnarwarre battery project in Victoria.

Samsung C&T described the project as a milestone moment for the company’s growing presence in the Australian energy market, adding it “showcases our global capabilities in delivering complex, grid-critical energy infrastructure.”

The local developer arm of Samsung, Samsung C&T Renewable Energy Australia, is advancing a multi-gigawatt pipeline of renewable energy generation and storage projects across New South Wales, Queensland, and Victoria, led by the 200 MW/800 MWh Darnum and the 100 MW / 400 MWh Mangoplah BESS. It also received approval for the South Coree project, a 80 MW / 320 MWh BESS, last month.

item.title: Longi unveils 690 W back-contact solar module with 25.54% efficiency
item.dc:creator: Vincent Shaw
item.description: Longi has introduced its Hi-MO X12 back-contact solar modules, featuring an integrated conductive backsheet that replaces conventional soldered ribbons with metal foil circuits. The company claims the design eliminates more than 15,000 potential solder-joint failure points per module, improves current-carrying capacity and increases power output by 6 W to 8 W.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese solar module manufacturer Longi has unveiled its Hi-MO X12 module series. The new back-contact modules target residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) rooftop solar applications, with a focus on power density, interconnection design and long-term reliability.

The Hi-MO X12 series is based on Longi’s hybrid passivated back contact (HPBC) 2.0 cell technology and features an integrated conductive backsheet architecture that replaces conventional soldered ribbons with conductive metal foil circuits embedded in the rear encapsulation structure.

According to Longi, the design enables cells to connect directly to the conductive backsheet, eliminating more than 15,000 potential solder-joint failure points per module. The company said the architecture increases the current-carrying cross-sectional area by 85%, resulting in a power gain of 6 W to 8 W compared with conventional interconnection designs.

The modules also feature what Longi calls Full-Screen Technology, which combines shingled cell layouts with hidden busbars to reduce inactive areas and front-side shading losses. The manufacturer claims the design delivers an additional 8 W to 12 W, bringing the total power gain to between 14 W and 20 W.

The larger-format LR7-72WVD module for C&I applications is available in power ratings ranging from 660 W to 690 W, with a maximum module efficiency exceeding 25.54%, according to the manufacturer.

The smaller LR7-54WVD series is available in four power classes ranging from 495 W to 510 W, with module efficiencies of 24.25% to 24.99% under standard test conditions, according to the product datasheet.

The 108-cell, dual-glass LR7-54WVD module measures 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weighs 23.5 kg. It features a black anodised aluminum frame and front and rear semi-tempered glass layers measuring 2.0 mm and 1.6 mm thick, respectively.

The module has a temperature coefficient of -0.26%/C, an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C and a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V. The datasheet specifies front and rear static load ratings of 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively, as well as resistance to impacts from 25 mm hailstones traveling at 23 m/s.

Longi said the new interconnection design also improves mechanical durability. The company claims its ultra-thin stacking process reduces internal stress by 60%, while an integrated metal foil barrier reduces water vapor transmission by 90%.

The LR7-54WVD series comes with a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year performance warranty. Longi guarantees maximum first-year degradation of 1%, followed by annual degradation of 0.35%, corresponding to approximately 88.9% of the initial power output after 30 years.

The product datasheet lists IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 among the applicable certification standards and includes certification marks from TÜV Rheinland and TÜV SÜD.

Longi has not disclosed Australian pricing, initial shipment volumes or a commercial delivery schedule for the Hi-MO X12 series.

At the same event, the manufacturer also introduced its Hi-MO 9 Prime utility-scale module and showcased its LongiBank 3.0 and OneMatrix energy storage solutions, alongside the Longi Block modular PV system.

item.title: Pacific inks offtake agreement for battery retrofit project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Pacific Partnerships is pushing ahead with plans to build a 102 MW, four-hour battery alongside its 102 MW Glenrowan Solar Farm in Victoria’s northeast after finalising a 10-year offtake agreement for the project.
item.content:encoded:
Pacific Partnerships, the renewable energy arm of Sydney-headquartered construction and engineering firm Cimic Group, has secured a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) with Victoria’s State Electricity Commission (SEC) for the Chivers Road battery project in northeast Victoria.

The 102 MW, four-hour battery energy storage system (BESS) is to be built on the site of Pacific’s 102 MW Glenrowan Solar Farm, located near the town of the same name in Victoria’s northeast.

Pacific said the Chivers Road BESS will connect to the site’s existing 33 kV grid infrastructure and bolster the solar farm’s capacity to store and dispatch renewable energy, supporting grid stability and maximising the benefits of solar generation.

The Glenrowan Solar Farm has been operating since early 2024 and is contracted through a long-term PPA with the SEC. The publicly-owned utility has now finalised a 10-year offtake agreement for the solar farm and battery project, replacing the existing arrangement.

Pacific General Manager David Lovell said the agreement builds on the success of the solar farm and creates the investment certainty required for the company to push ahead with the project.

“We look forward to similar success as we undertake our first large scale BESS hybridisation,” he said. “Our agreement with SEC provides an important foundation for progressing the battery towards construction and delivering future investment and employment opportunities in Victoria’s northeast.”

Construction of the Chivers Road battery is expected to commence in the coming weeks following financial close with the project expected to be operational from mid-2028.

The SEC, that has secured access to 65% of the battery’s output, said the project will add significant storage capacity to the state-owned utility’s growing energy portfolio, strengthening its ability to supply government, and commercial and industrial customers across Victoria.

“Energy storage is critical to ensuring our customers have access to affordable, reliable electricity when they need it,” SEC Chief Executive Officer Chris Miller said.

“This agreement will allow us to make better use of the solar energy generated during the day and strengthen our ability to supply customers during periods of high demand.”

“We are building a diverse portfolio that brings generation and storage together to support Victoria’s energy future.”

SEC supplies renewable electricity, backed by storage, to more than 4,400 sites across Victoria, meeting approximately 5% of the state’s total electricity demand. It has signed up to supply all Victorian government operations with 100% renewable energy.

It is targeting 4.5 GW of committed energy generation and storage assets by 2035. The utility said it now has more than 1 GW of committed generation and storage assets and is now over 20% of the way towards its 2035 portfolio target.

item.title: MPower lands $250 million funding injection to fuel mid-scale solar and storage strategy
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian renewable energy developer MPower will accelerate the rollout of its pipeline of mid-scale solar and battery storage projects after securing a $250 million commitment from industry superannuation giant Rest Super.
item.content:encoded:
Superannuation fund Rest Super has confirmed it will provide $250 million (USD 176 million) in fresh funding that will allow MPower to accelerate the building out its project pipeline, with a focus on mid-scale solar and battery energy storage projects.

Sydney-based MPower, acquired by specialist climate investor Wollemi Capital last year in a $19 million deal, has established itself as a developer of mostly mid-scale solar farms and battery energy storage systems, based on the theory that projects of 5 MW or less can avoid some of the risks associated with large-scale projects, such as grid constraints, social licence concerns and planning delays.

The developer said these smaller projects typically have a much shorter lead time, a smaller development footprint and can utilise spare capacity within the network without requiring substantial new network infrastructure.

“Our model is built for speed,” the company said. “We build distributed, network-connected solar and battery storage that adds capacity where the grid needs it most, as the NEM moves from fossil fuels to renewables.”

MPower said since its acquisition by Wollemi, it has substantially scaled up its development activity, with solar and battery storage projects currently under construction across three states and a further project pipeline under active development.

The developer said the fresh injection of funds will allow it to take on new development opportunities at a much bigger scale.

Rest’s commitment follows an initial $100 million committed to MPower last year by Wollemi and takes the total capital committed to the platform to $350 million.

Wollemi co-Chief Executive Officer Paul Hunyor said the fresh funds significantly increase the scale at which MPower can pursue new development opportunities.

“This sets MPower up for its next phase of growth – more projects under construction, more batteries on the ground,” he said.

item.title: Clutch lands ARENA backing to drive battery manufacturing project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: An Australian-developed modular solid-state battery system designed for use at home, on the road and off-grid is moving towards scalable local manufacturing.
item.content:encoded:
Melbourne-based Clutch Industries has secured $6.77 million (USD 4.76 million) in funding through the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) to establish and operate a pilot manufacturing line for a portable 4 kWh battery pack built on solid-state battery architecture.

The $19.35 million project will focus on Clutch’s PowerNet – a modular 4 kWh battery pack the company said can operate independently or be combined with multiple units to create a home battery system. Units can also be detached and used as portable power sources.

“PowerNet is about rethinking how batteries are used, creating a modular, high-performance energy platform that can power everything from homes and off-grid systems to vehicles and marine applications,” the company said.

“This funding is an important step in turning that vision into reality.”

The project will see Clutch – through its new battery division Density – design, construct and commission a scalable manufacturing line at its facility in Coburg. The line will assemble pre-conditioned solid-state battery cells into complete PowerNet systems incorporating battery management, power electronics, mechanical protection and integrated energy interfaces.

The project will also test the batteries’ safety and performance across different uses, helping refine the product and meet the requirements needed to bring it to a wider market. 

Clutch, which has been engineering and manufacturing clutch systems since 1951, said most lithium-ion batteries contain a flammable liquid electrolyte inside each cell. The company said the cells in its batteries are without free-flowing liquid, providing increased safety and power while reducing weight.

Clutch said the project will help it move from product development into scalable Australian manufacturing and will support real-world validation and future commercial uptake of solid-state architecture that offers energy density up to 50% higher than conventional lithium-ion technology.

“As the world embraces electrification, we see enormous opportunities to apply our engineering and manufacturing experience to new technologies and markets,” the company said.

ARENA Chief Executive Officer Darren Miller said the project, funded through the federal government’s Battery Breakthrough Initiative, is an opportunity to turn promising battery technology into Australian manufacturing capability.

“A battery that can support a household and then be taken on the road shows how flexible and innovative energy storage technology is becoming,” he said.

“Projects like this can build Australian manufacturing skills and give locally developed energy technologies the opportunity to demonstrate their value at commercial scale.”

Clutch said it expects PowerNet will launch in early 2027.

Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the project will support the growth of the advanced battery manufacturing capability in Australia. 

“More Australians are choosing batteries to make the most of their solar and cut their power bills. We want Australian manufacturers and workers to share in that opportunity,” he said.

“This project is about making batteries here that people can use in their everyday lives, whether that’s storing energy at home or taking power with them on a camping trip, or their workplace.”

item.title: Australia needs workforce pipeline to deliver infrastructure rollout
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australia has spent years planning the infrastructure needed to enable the energy transition. We now need the same focus on the people and skills required to build it.
item.content:encoded:
As the nation accelerates investment in renewable energy and network infrastructure, the workforce responsible for building and maintaining this infrastructure is under increasing pressure. Apprentice numbers are declining, experienced workers are nearing retirement, and it can take close to a decade to develop a fully qualified, independent transmission line worker.

At the heart of the energy transition, transmission line workers build the infrastructure needed to take energy from where it is generated to the homes, communities, and businesses where it is needed.

AEMO’s 2026 Integrated System Plan identifies about 6,000 kilometres of new transmission in the National Electricity Market by 2050 under its Step Change scenario. A strong workforce will be essential to deliver that infrastructure and maintain it.

But apprentice numbers are falling across the industry, and many experienced workers are approaching retirement. It takes years to develop a fully qualified, independent transmission line worker. If we do not address the workforce challenge now, we risk losing both the skills and the knowledge needed to deliver the work ahead.

If we’re serious about the energy transition, then we need to get serious about addressing this and the broader workforce challenges the sector faces. To do this, we need to change how we recruit into the sector and foster new learning and mentoring opportunities.

Zinfra has continued to recruit and train apprentices, but no single employer can solve this challenge alone. Government, industry and training providers need to plan together for the workforce the energy transition will require.

This means broadening the way we recruit. Skills from other sectors, including emergency services, agriculture and defence, can transfer into energy roles. We should create more pathways for people with those skills to enter the industry.

We need to do more to attract women as well. Through targeted outreach and partnerships with organisations such as Empowered Women in Trades (EWIT), schools, TAFEs and community groups, Zinfra is working to make the opportunities across our sector better known.

The results are encouraging. Applications to our apprentice programs have grown by 250% in recent years. In 2025, applications from women increased by 81%. We are also seeing more people apply after changing careers.

Recruitment is only the first step. Training and knowledge transfer turn new starters into a capable workforce.

That means having enough training capacity for the people entering the industry and creating stronger pathways for experienced workers to become mentors and trainers. Their practical knowledge is one of the sector’s most valuable resources.

Zinfra has experienced the training-capacity challenge directly. When TAFE capacity for line worker training fell short of our needs, we provided three experienced professionals to support training at a Victorian education facility. It helped address the immediate shortfall, but a lasting solution requires a more sustainable approach.

So where do we go from here?

Australia already knows much of the infrastructure it will need years in advance. We need to bring the same long-term planning to the workforce required to deliver it.

That means aligning apprenticeship and training capacity with future infrastructure demand, opening pathways for career changers and underrepresented groups, and giving experienced workers a real incentive to pass on their knowledge.

Australia has the talent and capability to turn its energy ambitions into reality. We need to recruit beyond traditional sectors, open new pathways into the industry and help experienced workers train the next generation. That is how we make sure Australia’s energy future is not only planned but built.

Author: Peter Iancov, Managing Director, Zinfra

item.title: Sungrow unveils all-in-one battery system with built-in EV charger
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Sungrow has introduced an all-in-one inverter and battery stack for residential applications that supports up to 120 kWh storage capacity and has an EV charger built into it.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese manufacturer Sungrow’s new PowerHarbour Pro all-in-one residential energy storage system offers power ratings from 10 kW to 30 kW and battery modules from 7 kWh to 10 kWh, with total storage expandable up to 120 kWh. It also includes a built-in AC electric vehicle (EV) charger designed to support future V2X applications and offering 7 kW per phase.

A standard PowerHarbour, without the integrated EV charger, is also available.

Sungrow Australia Technical Service Director Scott Su said the platform has been designed to simplify energy management for Australian households, whether installing a new solar-plus-storage system or upgrading an existing setup.

“Australia’s transition towards more connected home energy systems presents a significant opportunity for the industry,” he said. “We believe the next step is not simply adding more features, but making solar, storage and energy management work together more effectively.”

“With PowerHarbour, our focus is on bringing these technologies together in a practical, flexible solution that can support different household needs as the market evolves.”

The platform’s energy storage is provided through a stackable battery system built on 314 Ah ultra-capacity LiFePO4 prismatic cells. Sungrow Chief Technical Support Engineer Graham Smith said this modular architecture enables flexible scaling through multiple battery module options.

“The inverter itself is from 5, 8 to 10 kW single phase and up to 30 kW in three phase,” he said. “You can stack up to six battery modules, which gives you up to 60 kWh of storage and you can parallel another stack the same so you can have up to 120 kWh of storage.”

The system supports up to 1.6 times standard PV-to-battery charging and operates across a temperature range of -20 C to 50 C, according to the company, and achieves a lifecycle of up to 10,000 cycles under 90% depth of discharge testing conditions, making it suitable for long-term residential energy storage applications. Both the inverter and battery units are rated IP66 and the system has an operating temperature range of -20 C to 50 C.

The PowerHarbour includes Sungrow’s EnergyBridge, a companion backup unit that integrates a changeover switch, circuit breaker, meter, bypass switch, and current transformer into a single device. Sungrow said the unit is up to 99% smaller by volume than a conventional backup gateway and can reduce installation time by up to one hour.

Smith said the system also pairs with the Sungrow’s iSolarCloud monitoring platform to simplify commissioning while offering homeowners real-time visibility into generation, storage, and consumption.

“The homeowners can have a look and get the real-time data,” he said. “The installer can also access it and if something is not quite right, the installer can use that for fault finding.”

“We can also use it and can dig down to cell levels with batteries. If there’s something wrong we can find it and quite often remotely fix the issue. If not, we can take it to the installer to replace.”

The PowerHarbour Pro is currently awaiting Clean Energy Council approval and is expected to be available for install in Australia in Q1 2027.

Sungrow said the integrated EV charger has been designed for future vehicle-to-everything (V2X) applications, although that functionality remains subject to market availability and compatibility.
